title: Weniger Kirchenaustritte in Kärnten
content:
Auch wenn sich die Religionslandschaft in den letzten Jahrzehnten stark verändert hat, bekennt sich mit knapp 56 Prozent immer noch mehr als die Hälfte der Kärntnerinnen und Kärntner zur Katholischen Kirche. Und die Zahl jener, die der Kirche den Rücken kehren, ist weiter gesunken.
Weniger Kirchenaustritte in Kärnten
Die Katholische Kirche Österreich hat am Mittwoch ihre Bilanz für das vergangene Jahr veröffentlicht. Neben dem Rechnungsabschluss stehen dabei auch immer die Kirchenaustritte im Fokus. Diese sind, wie schon in den Jahren davor, neuerlich zurückgegangen. Österreichweit und auch in Kärnten.
Sedlmaier: Menschen suchen Halt
Im vergangenen Jahr gab es 3.881 Kirchenaustritte, das ist ein Minus von 15 Prozent gegenüber 2024. Österreichweit liegt der Rückgang bei sechs Prozent. Gleichzeitig sind auch mehr Menschen wieder- oder neu in die Katholische Kirche eingetreten, nämlich 495. Im Jahr 2024 waren es 440. Seit einem Jahr ist das auch online möglich. „Ich bin geradezu glücklich darüber, dass sich diese Zahlen so positiv entwickelt haben und das ist für mich ein klares Zeichen dafür, dass Glaube und Kirche für das Leben unserer Menschen im Land eine große Bedeutung hat“, so Generalvikar Johann Sedlmaier.
Eine Rolle dürften hier wohl auch die aktuellen Krisen und Kriege spielen. „Menschen suchen natürlich in unsicheren Zeiten Halt und Ankerpunkte, wo sie sich orientieren können. Ich denke, die Kirche ist so ein Kraftort“, so Sedlmaier.
Plus im Rechnungsabschluss
Der Rückgang bei den Austritten wirkt sich auch auf die Finanzen der Kirche aus. Drei Viertel der Einnahmen stammen aus dem Kirchenbeitrag. Und so weist der Rechnungsabschluss für 2025 Jahr ein leichtes Plus aus. Angesichts steigender Kosten muss aber weiter gespart werden, unter anderem auch bei den Mitarbeitern. „In Summe versuchen wir einen Mitarbeiterstand auch zukünftig so zu entwickeln, dass wir nicht jede Position nachbesetzen und dass wir auf Basis einer hohen Flexibilität unserer Kolleginnen und Kollegen auch intern umschichten und die ein oder andere Position natürlich dann auch von außen dazukommt“, so der Direktor der Finanzkammer Gerhard Salzer.
Derzeit hat die Katholische Kirche Kärnten 722 Mitarbeiter, darunter 197 aktive Priester, die von etwa 40 Priestern, die bereits in Pension sind, unterstützt werden.

title: Civil registration drive helps fix gaps in vital records
content: Philomene Nyirambabazi believed all her five children were properly registered after birth. But when the resident of Nyamugari Cell in Gasaka Sector, Nyamagabe District took them for photographs as part of the ongoing digital identity registration exercise, she discovered that her youngest child, an eight-year-old, had never been registered in the civil registration system. ALSO READ: Relief as Rwanda eases registration of births She was directed to the cell office, where the child was registered and given a number to proceed with digital ID registration. “I thought all my children had been registered, but it turned out that some were not. The civil registration services they brought closer to us have been very helpful,” Nyirambabazi said. She is among citizens who have used the ongoing civil registration exercise to register children, correct errors in their records and access other services. The exercise was held as Rwanda marked African Civil Registration Day and officially launched Civil Registration Week under the theme “Proper civil registration, the foundation of quality services.” The week is intended to help citizens who have not accessed civil registration services, including those who have not registered their children, while also allowing people to correct errors in their existing records. ALSO READ: Civil registration is an obligation and right of every Rwandan – Mukabaramba The activity also included photographing citizens for the Single Digital ID, with local authorities assisting residents to resolve issues identified in their civil registration records. Minister of Local Government Dominique Habimana, who was in Nyamagabe to officially launch civil registration week, said accurate civil registration is essential for both citizens and national development. “For us to achieve the development we aspire to, the country needs to have a clear record of its population and accurate demographic statistics,” Habimana said. He said such information enables government to properly plan for infrastructure and public services, including schools, health facilities, water and electricity, as well as settlement planning. Rwanda has also digitised several civil registration services to make them easier and faster to access. Citizens can obtain documents through Irembo platform without having to travel long distances or spend a full day at government offices. Birth and death registration services are provided at health facilities and cell offices free of charge, while an electronic system known as e-Death Notification allows village leaders to report deaths electronically. ALSO READ: Citizens urged on timely registration of death, birth events Habimana encouraged citizens and local leaders to make use of the system. Other civil registration services, including marriage registration, child recognition and establishing parentage, are provided at sector level and at Rwandan embassies abroad. The minister also encouraged couples living together without being legally married to approach local authorities and formalise their union, saying this has benefits for the couples, their children and the family as a whole. The ongoing exercise has also enabled residents to identify errors in information already contained in the civil registration system. Rafael Munyaneza, a resident of Kabacuzi Village in Nyamagabe Cell, brought two of his children to be photographed for the digital ID when he discovered errors in their records. One child had been recorded as having been born in Gitega Sector, Nyarugenge District, while the other had an incorrect date of birth. The errors were corrected within minutes before the children were photographed. ALSO READ: Digitisation takes centre stage as Rwanda launches civil registration week Munyaneza said he understood that having accurate personal information in the system makes it easier to access key services, including those related to marriage and property transactions. “When your civil registration records are in order, it speeds up every service you need related to civil registration,” he said. The activities were held in Nyamagabe, which was recognised as the best-performing district nationally in civil registration services during the 2025/26 financial year. The district scored 95.4 percent, followed by Nyarugenge with 95.3 percent, Gicumbi at 94.7 percent, Gakenke at 94.6 percent and Ruhango at 93.8 percent. The ranking was based on districts’ average performance in birth registration, death registration and verbal autopsy between July 2025 and July 2026. Minister Habimana presented Nyamagabe Mayor Hildebrand Niyomwungeri with an award recognising the district’s performance. Niyomwungeri attributed the result to awareness campaigns and efforts by residents and local officials to improve access to civil registration services. He, however, said limited access to digital technology and internet connectivity sometimes delay services, while some cases require citizens to go through the justice system. He said the district would continue working to address the challenges and improve service delivery.

title: At this Indianapolis middle school, student mediators help drive down suspensions
content:
Sign up for Chalkbeat Indiana’s free daily newsletter to keep up with Indianapolis Public Schools, Marion County’s township districts, and statewide education news.
Sixth grader Jocelyn Montiel had her phone stolen. She said her friend, Esteban Gonzalez, was to blame.
Gathered around a table in educator Grover Edwards’ classroom, the two students discussed the situation with two of their peers who were serving as mediators.
Jocelyn shared her sense of betrayal when she turned around to find her phone gone. Esteban described the injustice of being falsely accused.
The two mediators restated the issue and asked Esteban directly if he stole the phone.
They redirected the students when they started raising their voices and helped each reflect on what they could have done differently.
The fight over the phone was only a simulation — in fact, Jocelyn and Esteban serve as mediators too. The conflict resolution methods the students were practicing are part of a decade-old peer mediation program at H.L. Harshman Middle School, which enrolls about 500 students on the near eastside of Indianapolis. Through the program, students learn how to help their classmates settle disputes before they escalate, leading to a better school climate. School leaders say it has contributed to fewer fights and suspensions, even as statewide out-of-school suspension rates hover above pre-pandemic levels.
Student mediators say friends and classmates seek out mediation as an alternative to fighting. In mediation, students put their feelings into words in a supportive environment.
“Talking to an adult, you may be getting in trouble,” said Isabell Gonzales, an eighth grader who has been part of the program since sixth grade. “When you’re talking to your peers there’s less pressure.”
What issues does middle school peer mediation tackle?
The program is supported by a $1.2 million grant from Indiana University Health that places Peace Learning Center trainers in IPS and Lawrence Township classrooms to teach mediators how to resolve middle school conflicts. Similar approaches have been used in New York City schools and elsewhere.
Harshman leaders contacted the Peace Learning Center about starting a peer mediation program in 2016, but the program took off after the IU Health donation and when the school hired Edwards, said Tim Nation, executive director of the Peace Learning Center. Edwards has been leading the program for six years.
Peer mediation is meant to address conflicts before they turn into physical confrontations that require adult intervention. Students most commonly seek mediation for fights between friends or conflicts over relationships, the mediators said. Those kinds of conflicts can be trickier to resolve than determining who took a phone, they added.
“When it comes to relationships, it’s harder for people to take accountability for what they did or said,” said seventh grader Camille Hynes.
One of the hardest parts of learning how to mediate is helping their peers find the words to express how they feel, said Jocelyn, whose older sister also served as a peer mediator.
“Sometimes people will agree with what we’re saying just to get it over with,” Camille said.
Still, it can be easier to express feelings to a peer than a teacher or administrator, Jocelyn said.
More than 100 students applied to be mediators this year, but only about 25 to 30 were selected after an interview process, said Edwards. They train for three weeks after school before stepping in to mediate conflicts.
“They want to be a part of something, building something stronger,” he said.
Harshman students can seek mediation by filling out a form in Edwards’ classroom, where posters about peace line the walls and cloth drapes dim the fluorescent lighting.
Edwards said he has seen a significant drop in the number of fights breaking out in Harshman hallways, as well as subsequent suspensions.
Discipline data from the Richard M. Fairbanks Foundation shows that Harshman’s out-of-school suspension rate began declining in 2016 before spiking shortly after the pandemic.
Since 2023, the share of students with out-of-school suspensions has declined from a peak of 26% to 8% in 2024-25.
Across IPS, the out-of-school suspension rate has remained around 10% since 2022, lower than before the pandemic. About 6.5% of students statewide had an out-of-school suspension last year, slightly higher than before the pandemic.
Over the last school year, peer mediators handled about 25 peer conflicts, Edwards said.
Edwards also facilitated conferences with students focused on restorative practices, which are alternatives to traditional discipline focused on repairing harm.
Students and teachers must trust the process
When a conflict is resolved, both parties sign an agreement not to discuss their argument further outside the room. That helps build trust in the mediation process and mitigates feelings of embarrassment, the mediators said.
“Talking about it after can become a further issue,” Camille said. “The situation may be small but that can make it bigger.”
The program also requires buy-in from adults at the school, Principal Amy Moore said. Administrators have to trust that the peer mediators can resolve a conflict using the skills they’ve learned.
The principles of peer mediation have had an effect beyond Edwards’ classroom, she said.
Moore said she sees students in the hallways using conflict resolution language with each other. They say in jest: “That’s not the Harshman way,” she said.
“They’ve internalized it,” Moore said. “It’s become woven into the fabric of the school.”
Aleksandra Appleton covers Indiana education policy and writes about K-12 schools across the state. Contact her at aappleton@chalkbeat.org.

title: For Quincy's Chinese community, the American dream lives on, with caveats
content:
For Quincy's Chinese community, the American dream lives on, with caveats
When Ziqiang Yuan moved to the U.S. in 1999, democracy was the last thing on her mind. Political speech was suppressed under socialist rule in her native China, and her aversion to politics stayed with her when she emigrated.
“We have a saying in China, ‘不谈政治.’ That means, ‘don't talk about politics,’ ” Yuan said. “You can get in trouble.”
Yuan, 55, goes by Susan now. She left Wuhan for the U.S. to pursue a post-doc in biomedical research, a field that then offered few opportunities in China while demand here was high. She even landed a scholarship.
But when her landlady brought Yuan to a local municipal meeting, eager to show the young grad student what American democracy looked like, something changed in Yuan. She was impressed that ordinary people were even aware of government gatherings, let alone that they could attend.
“That city council meeting really opened my eyes,” Yuan said. “You can have a chance to speak — directly speak — to those officials.”
Decades later, that first brush with local government would lead Yuan to try her chances at politics, a pathway she couldn’t have imagined had she stayed in China.
Yuan is among 175,000 people of Chinese descent who call Massachusetts home, including one in six Quincy residents. For most of U.S. history, Chinese immigrants have journeyed here in hopes of a better life. Their aspirations have varied decade to decade, and person to person. Indeed, ask people in Quincy about the American dream and the answers are as varied as the food options along Hancock and Beale streets.
Interviews with Chinese immigrants spanning multiple generations suggest the allure of the U.S. is being put to the test, amid a torrent of immigration restrictions under President Trump and the emergence of China as the world’s second-largest economy. But for many, the core draw of America remains strong, whether that’s for greater wealth, liberty or cultural freedoms that are elusive in China.
The ’80s generation
On a recent weekend in a downtown event space in Quincy, seniors in classical Chinese attire acted out the myth of the immortal moon goddess.
The Mid-Autumn Festival celebration was organized by Frank Poon of the nonprofit Civic Education Alliance. Poon came to the U.S. during a wave of Chinese immigration in the 1980s. Ronald Reagan was president, Beijing relaxed restrictions on its citizens’ ability to leave the country and the British would agree to transfer Hong Kong to Chinese control.
Poon said he knows success in the U.S. is far from guaranteed — and it often takes a lifetime of struggle.
“We’re still aiming at the American dream,” Poon said, and that people like him are “willing to invest all our time, all our effort, to make it come true.”
Looking back, Poon said he’s achieved what brought him to America 43 years ago. For him, that success has been more spiritual than something that can be measured.
“My American dream is, ‘I want to have a better life,’ ” he said. “I do have a better family. I do have opportunity to work with the community, and deep inside, in my heart and soul, I feel good.”
But one attendee of the harvest festival had something to say about a dream deferred.
In 1988, Carol Chu followed her future husband to Boston, with little money and no family here.
“The United States is such a freedom country,” she said. “I wanted to enjoy all the opportunity — get the chance to be free, live free, speak freely.”
Soon after they settled, however, Chu began to realize those things might be out of reach. She became pregnant, and her husband developed a severe gambling addiction. The worst part was when Chu lost custody of her son.
“I [was] so disappointed when I came here, because my American dream totally has not come true,” she said.
Instead of returning to her country, Chu stayed in the U.S. in order to be with her son, even if she could only see him one hour at a time.
"The United States is such a freedom country. I wanted to enjoy all the opportunity — get the chance to be free, live free, speak freely."
Carol Chu
Chu recently retired after 37 years working for the Postal Service, and as the years have brought her closer to her son, she said she is finally happy here. Now that her boy is grown, Chu plans to split her time between China and the U.S.
“I think my duty is done,” she said.
Over the decades since these folks emigrated to the U.S., China has roared forward as an economic titan, with hundreds of millions emerging from extreme poverty. For the Chinese youth of today, that adds a new dimension to the decision to leave, whether for the U.S. or anywhere else in the world.
The next generation
At Quincy’s Wollaston Beach, dozens of Chinese youth spread out on the sand, playing mahjong and practicing the Cantonese language. It was a meetup of the Boston Cantonese Club, and DJ Amanda Lou was spinning pop music under a tent.
The recent Boston University graduate is from Macau, a special administrative region of China ruled by the Portuguese until 1999. She spoke about the American ideal more in terms of culture than economic opportunities or political freedom. For her and many other Chinese graduates, Lou said, the exposure to freedom and different lifestyles is a strong motivation to stay.
“In Boston, I can just wear whatever I want, right? I can wear a tank top, shorts, walk outside — nothing will change," she said. "No one's going to stare at you."
At 23, Lou is ready to make a life in Boston. But remaining in the U.S. has never been a certainty for international students. It depends on factors like finding an employer to sponsor a visa petition. And with the current administration looking to add massive fees for foreign worker visas — and to favor “higher-skilled and higher-paid” applicants — big challenges loom for people like Lou.
“What happens if I don't find an employer who's willing to sponsor me?” she said. “Even if they do, what happens if I get fired or something? Definitely very stressful.”
Lou hopes to open a jazz bar in Boston one day, but if America is out of reach, she’ll have to bring her dreams elsewhere.
This kind of uncertainty is well-known to Vincent Lau, an immigration attorney in Boston. Much of his work involves helping American companies secure work visas. Lau said the traditional legal routes still exist, but they have increasingly narrowed under President Trump.
Among an array of measures to tighten rules on student immigration, Lau said consular officers now hold greater discretion to deny visa petitions, making it more difficult to advise parents on the wisdom of sending their kids to the U.S.
“Applying for the visas at the consulates has become much more challenging for Chinese citizens in general,” Lau said, “especially for students.”
On top of that, the administration is cutting research funding and suing elite universities, which Lau said have long been reliable paths to success in America. The administration has threatened to revoke visas for some Chinese students, and it accused Harvard of collaborating with the Chinese Communist Party.
Lau said the draw to study and live in the U.S. remains strong, but those policies are taking a toll.
“When [universities] are not being backed by the government, when they are being attacked by the government, it's not a quote-unquote, safe place,” Lau said. “It's not a place where people want to go.”
The impetus to immigrate has also changed as Chinese universities rise in global rankings. More Chinese youth are pursuing their studies in China. At the same time, an increasing number of students are returning home after graduating overseas.
But for Boston Cantonese Club organizer Alex Ng, China is no promised land. Ng said the Chinese tech economy suffers from a "race to the bottom" mentality, more driven by the search for rock bottom prices than by innovation. Ng said competition for jobs is fiercer in China than in the U.S., and that's especially hard for college grads.
“There are a lot of scientific and technology breakthroughs in China. I'm not discounting that,” said Ng, who holds a master’s in electrical engineering from MIT. “But on the other side, a lot of people graduate from college, they just cannot get a job.”
Born in Hong Kong, Ng moved to Boston from Toronto four years ago. He considers himself lucky that he got his work visa when Joe Biden was president; he worries his peers will now have a harder time.
Ng has yet to achieve his goals of getting married and starting a business. But among his options — and for all this country’s imperfections — Ng said the United States is the place to be. The prestige of the American dream persists, even for a Chinese immigrant who grew up just north of the border.
“First of all, we don't have any Canadian dream,” Ng said with a laugh. “But in Canada, we always heard of the term American dream.”
While many immigrants, like Ng, feel that dream is still a thing, others caution that in one principle area, America could be slipping.
'Liberty is precious'
Sitting outside a Quincy church where two U.S. presidents are interred, Susan Yuan reflected on her path to politics.
After eight years doing research at the University of Vermont and Dartmouth College, she decided to leave academia. She moved to Quincy, and eventually took a job at the Quincy public library.
Soon news out of City Hall started to get under her skin. The council approved a 79% pay hike for the mayor in 2024, and Yuan helped organize a ballot petition to reverse the raise. She was a city employee at the time, and people asked her if she feared retaliation.
“This is America. People should have a right to speak and to petition,” Yuan said. “That's what I learned when I came to U.S.”
"Honestly, I never planned to become a public official. And I don't think that could happen if I'm still in China. So, by that sense, it is a kind of American dream, even though I never dreamed about it."
Yuan’s experience with grassroots activism led her to run for Quincy councilor-at-large. She considered herself a longshot. But she became part of an anti-incumbent wave in the city, and in January, she was sworn in alongside five other new councilors promising to bring change to the city.
“Honestly, I never planned to become a public official,” she said. “And I don't think that could happen if I'm still in China. So, by that sense, it is a kind of American dream, even though I never dreamed about it.”
But Yuan said she worries the U.S. is showing signs of the authoritarianism she left behind.
At the Sept. 8 meeting of the Quincy City Council, dozens of residents showed up to protest the police department's use of Flock Safety’s automated license plate reader cameras. The technology has received pushback from around the country following allegations of misuse by officers, as well as fears the data could be used for immigration enforcement.
Yuan was the first councilor at the meeting to express concern over what she described as a lack of transparency by the city.
“As an immigrant who came from a country in a centralized government, I want to tell you, liberty is precious,” she told the council. “As John Adams said, ‘Liberty once lost is lost forever.’ "
Yuan’s proposal — to hold a hearing on the city’s use of Flock cameras — passed unanimously.
In an interview, Yuan said she experienced mass surveillance during recent visits to China, with cameras watching from all angles. Yuan said surveillance has become so ubiquitous there that some people don’t bother to complain, perhaps because they feel powerless to make change.
“When we see U.S. start to head into that direction, we are more vigilant,” she said.
Now, she wants to help make sure the same doesn’t happen in America. The fact that people are pushing back on surveillance, on the left and the right, she said is a good sign.
This segment aired on September 23, 2026.

title: Six TVET schools benefit from Rwf16bn infrastructure project
content: The Rwanda TVET Board (RTB) has inaugurated new and rehabilitated infrastructure worth €10 million (about Rwf16 billion) at six Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) schools across the country. The facilities were developed under the third phase of the RTB-KfW TVET Project, a partnership between the governments of Rwanda and Germany, with funding provided through Germany’s development bank, KfW. The inauguration ceremony took place at Busasamana Technical Secondary School (TSS) in Nyanza District on September 23. It was attended by the Minister of State for Education, Claudette Irere, and Germany’s Ambassador to Rwanda, Heike Uta Dettmann. The project involved the construction and rehabilitation of student dormitories, dining facilities, classrooms and workshops to improve learning and living conditions for TVET students. The six beneficiary schools are Busasamana TSS in Nyanza District, ES Kinazi TSS in Ruhango District, Father Ramon TSS in Kamonyi District, Karengera TSS in Nyamasheke District, St Augustin Mibirizi TSS in Rusizi District, and ETO Gatumba TSS in Ngororero District. ALSO READ: Govt partners with German institutions to promote TVET Speaking at the ceremony, Irere said the investment goes beyond infrastructure development, describing it as an investment in young people and their ability to contribute to the country's development. She said the partnership has enabled Rwanda to improve infrastructure, provide modern training equipment and strengthen training capacity across key technical secondary schools. However, she emphasised that the new facilities must translate into better training and improved preparation of students for employment and entrepreneurship. “A modern workshop is only valuable when it helps students develop the skills and confidence required to succeed. State-of-the-art tools and equipment only make a difference when learners know how to use them safely, effectively, and creatively,” she said. “Our responsibility is therefore clear. This investment must lead to measurable improvements in the quality of training and, ultimately, in students’ readiness for the labour market and entrepreneurship.” Irere said the government expects graduates to use their acquired skills not only to seek employment but also to develop solutions and establish businesses. “We wish to see young people leave these schools not simply searching for opportunities, but equipped with the tools and capabilities to create solutions, build enterprises, secure decent employment, and contribute meaningfully to their own development as well as that of the country,” she said. ALSO READ: Rwanda secures over $100m to set up TVET centres of excellence The minister urged school managers, instructors and local leaders to ensure the facilities are properly used and maintained to benefit future generations of learners. “Every classroom, workshop, machine, and piece of equipment must be properly used and carefully maintained so that they can serve not only today’s learners but generations of young learners to come,” she said. She also called on instructors to adopt modern teaching practices and ensure training programmes respond to changing industry needs. “Modern equipment must be matched by modern teaching practices, close supervision, and training that responds to the changing needs of various industries,” she said. Addressing students, Irere urged them to make the most of the opportunities provided by the investment. “Make the most of this opportunity, work hard, master your chosen profession, and uphold the highest ethical and professional standards,” she said. Germany pledges continued support for TVET Ambassador Dettmann welcomed the completion of the rehabilitation works, highlighting the importance of improved facilities, including kitchens and bathrooms, to students' daily lives. She said cooperation between Rwanda and Germany in technical and vocational education has a long history and draws on Germany's dual vocational training system, which combines classroom learning with practical workplace training. Dettmann said the completion of the third phase does not mark the end of the partnership. “The rehabilitation is complete, but as we have seen during the signing ceremony, the cooperation is not finished,” she said. “We will continue. We will concentrate on Rwanda because this is how Germany works. In our partnership, we take the lead from Rwanda.” RTB Director General Paul Umukunzi said the board is also implementing the fourth and fifth phases of the project, which have a combined value of €29 million (about Rwf48 billion). He said RTB has also signed a new agreement with KfW for a €16 million (about Rwf26 billion) project aimed at supporting young girls to pursue TVET studies and develop their skills. The completion of the third phase brings the total number of schools supported under the programme to 19, following five schools in the first phase and eight in the second. Busasamana boarding capacity more than doubles Elyse Mwumvaneza, head teacher of Busasamana TSS, said the new facilities have significantly increased the school's capacity to accommodate students. “Before this building was constructed, we used to receive 170 students in boarding, but now the number has increased to 430,” he said. The newly constructed dining hall can accommodate 500 students, while the boys' dormitory has a capacity of 168 students and the girls' dormitory can accommodate 120. Mwumvaneza said the expanded facilities will enable the school to accommodate more learners and provide a better environment for technical and vocational training.

title: “Entregamos vivienda social nueva que cuesta tres veces menos” que en el mercado”: Brugada
content:
“Entregamos vivienda social nueva que cuesta tres veces menos” que en el mercado”: Brugada
Expuso que su administración ha adquirido “en condiciones de mucha disputa y tensión por el suelo en estos 2 años, 250 mil metros cuadrados para construir vivienda”.
Al participar en la Cumbre de Alcaldes Urban 20 en Nueva York, U20, la jefa de gobierno, Clara Brugada, expresó que su administración está entregando vivienda social nueva que cuesta tres veces menos de lo que vale en el mercado.
Viviendas por menos de 50 mil dólares -860 mil pesos- en zonas donde cuestan ya entre 150 y 200 mil dólares -entre 2 millones 580 mil pesos y 3 millones 440 mil pesos- y en este año arrancamos una empresa pública de construcción de vivienda” dijo en la cumbre en la que participa el alcalde de Nueva York, Zohran Mamdani y el de Barcelona, Jaume Collboni, entre otros.
Brugada expuso que su administración ha adquirido “en condiciones de mucha disputa y tensión por el suelo en estos 2 años, 250 mil metros cuadrados para construir vivienda”.
Se refirió a la estrategia que llevan a cabo a través del Instituto de la Vivienda de la Ciudad de México, INVI, y comentó que entregan créditos a tasa cero a las familias trabajadoras “cuya devolución de este crédito no supera el 20 por ciento de sus ingresos”.
Y expuso que la política de vivienda de su administración es una política de democratización del crédito, de inclusión financiera a quienes históricamente han sido excluidos de la banca tradicional.
Y también se ha incrementado la construcción de vivienda ecológica, dijo la mandataria quien habló de que se han instalado 16 mil sistemas de captación de agua de lluvia, calentadores solares y huertos urbanos.
Y narró que como muchas familias recurren a la autoconstrucción a veces “no tienen techo o tienen grandes problemas porque la familia crece y necesitan la ampliación. Así que mejoramos la habitabilidad de la vivienda para cumplir con el precepto del derecho a una vivienda digna”, hasta el momento se han mejorado 40 mil viviendas que tenían estos problemas.

title: Introducing Nurse Navigators to Improve Pain Management in the Community.
content: Chronic pain among adults is a highly prevalent condition characterized by persistent gaps in care delivery, inequitable access to evidence-based interventions, and variable care continuity across clinical settings. Nurse Navigators are strategically positioned to help eliminate barriers by assisting in care coordination and person-centered resource maximization. A community-based nurse-led telehealth pilot program was implemented in the Northwestern United States as an extension of a state-funded evidence-based, online platform designed to promote nonpharmacologic pain management options and opioid risk reduction. This initiative offered structured one-to-one virtual consultations and facilitated use of digital self-assessment and educational resources. A convenience sample of adults (≥18 years) with self-reported chronic pain of at least 3 months' duration was recruited via email listservs. Eligible participants completed an initial videoconference session with a Pain Nurse Navigator and a follow-up session 10-14 days later. Ten adults (80% female; mean age 65) with chronic pain participated and completed the follow-up survey. Most either agreed or strongly agreed that they felt comfortable in the sessions with the Pain Nurse Navigator (100%) and were satisfied with the ease of participation (100%) and level of support (90%) provided by the Pain Nurse Navigator. The median Client Satisfaction Questionnaire-8 score was 26, indicating acceptable levels of satisfaction for the program. This pilot project established that a nurse-led pain navigation program can be delivered to adults living in a community setting, is acceptable to participants, and generated sufficient satisfaction scores to warrant further study. The model may be adaptable in other settings pending outcome evaluation.

title: Earn nothing? Pay nothing: 81-year-old Ahmedabad doctor charges patients based on their monthly income
content:
What if the amount you pay for a doctor’s consultation depended on how much you earn?
An 81-year-old ENT surgeon in Ahmedabad, Dr Nandlal Manseta, follows an unconventional fee system that allows patients to pay based on their income. Those with no income can consult him for free.
At his clinic, Manseta follows a simple sliding-scale model. Patients are not asked to submit income certificates or any other documents. Instead, the fee is decided on the basis of what they earn, with patients depositing the amount in a small donation box at the clinic.
According to the fee chart displayed at the clinic, someone earning Rs 1,000 pays Rs 10 for a consultation, while a monthly income of Rs 10,000 corresponds to a Rs 100 fee. Those earning Rs 1 lakh pay Rs 1,000. For patients with no income, the consultation is free.
Manseta follows this practice as part of his effort to give back to society. His approach is rooted in the belief that a person’s financial situation should not prevent them from seeking medical care.
View this post on Instagram
The doctor has also spoken about how support from society and the government played an important role in his own journey. He now tries to pay it forward.
The Better India recently shared Manseta’s story on social media. An overlay on the post featured one of his quotes: “If a patient’s income is zero, the fee is zero too.”
The story has since sparked a strong response online, with several users praising the doctor for making consultations more accessible.
“What a relief to patients who can’t afford to pay, but have Doctors like him who believe in treating patients. God bless him,” one user wrote.
“The ones with max income act the most privilidged don’t pay and create more fuss also,” another commented.
“Best thing is written below ‘no income proof needed’. Honesty is contagious,” a third user said.
“Even thousands of patients surgery were funded by manseta sir foundation,” another person shared.

title: Support from the U.S. Provides Food and Wheelchairs to Elderly in Camagüey
content:
A shipment containing essential supplies like food and wheelchairs has been dispatched from the United States to assist the elderly residents of the Monseñor Adolfo Home in Camagüey. This initiative has been made possible through generous donations from a Florida-based company, devoted Catholic followers, and members of the Camagüeyan exile community.
Details about this humanitarian effort were shared on Facebook by a page associated with the Monseñor Adolfo Home. The post extended gratitude to all those who facilitated the delivery of the container.
The food supplies were significantly contributed by Juan and Rosa Guixens of Guixens Food Group, a U.S. company specializing in the import and distribution of ethnic food products.
Founded in Florida in 1993, Guixens Food Group is headquartered in Miami and is recognized as a family-owned business. Besides its main operations in Miami, the company also maintains commercial activities in other U.S. locations, including Tampa, Atlanta, and New Jersey.
“Our heartfelt thanks to everyone who helped send this container filled with food and wheelchairs for the elderly at our Monseñor Adolfo Home in Camagüey,” the Facebook post stated.
The message specifically acknowledged Juan and Rosa Guixens “for the invaluable pallets of food” and the Catholic faithful who contributed the wheelchairs.
The post also highlighted the involvement of the board and members of the Municipality of Camagüey in Exile, a Florida-registered organization connected to the Camagüeyan community residing in Miami. Their donation was crucial in making the shipment possible.
“May God return this generosity in health and blessings and fill you with joy for doing a good deed,” the message concluded.
This aid arrives at a particularly challenging time for many elderly Cubans, who are struggling with inadequate pensions, high food prices, and shortages of basic necessities.
Earlier this year, it was reported that several social dining facilities for the elderly continued to operate thanks to donations coordinated by Catholic organizations.
One such donation enabled the distribution of nearly 1,000 kilograms of chickpeas across seven dining facilities in Havana, Camagüey, and Matanzas.
Despite their efforts, churches and religious organizations have faced obstacles.
In early September, a pastor from the municipality of Minas reported that authorities prevented his congregation from distributing breakfasts to the elderly and sick in the streets, forcing beneficiaries to travel to the church to receive their meals.
FAQs about Humanitarian Aid to Camagüey's Elderly
Who contributed to the shipment of food and wheelchairs to Camagüey?
The shipment was made possible by donations from a Florida-based company, Guixens Food Group, Catholic faithful, and members of the Camagüeyan exile community.
What challenges are elderly Cubans currently facing?
Elderly Cubans are dealing with insufficient pensions, high food prices, and shortages of essential goods, making daily life increasingly difficult.
How has the Guixens Food Group contributed to this cause?
Guixens Food Group, founded in Miami, contributed a significant portion of the food supplies sent to Camagüey, showcasing their commitment to helping those in need.

title: TOLIARA - L’axe principal de la ville réhabilité
content: Les gros trous qui parsemaient la chaussée aux abords du stationnement de Sanfily ne sont désormais plus qu’un mauvais souvenir. En période de pluies, de l’eau stagnante atteignant jusqu’aux hanches a fait le calvaire des usagers de la rue et des voyageurs qui prennent les taxi-brousses, qui n’ont pas eu le choix que de se tremper dans l’eau pour rejoindre les véhicules. Sanfily est en effet le principal stationnement de Toliara où les véhicules mini-car de marque Sprinter et Crafter, mais également les camions taxi-brousse ou « karandalana » se côtoient nuit et jour pour desservir l’axe Nord vers la RN9, l’Est-sud vers la RN10 et le Centre-est vers la RN7. C’est ainsi un axe principal par lequel passe la RN7 qui finit un kilomètre plus loin, au jardin de la mer de Toliara. RénovationLes habitants des quartiers d’Andabizy, de Motombe, d’Ankilimarovahatse, de Sanfily et d’Andakoro passent par Sanfily pour rejoindre la ville, pour ramener les élèves ou pour aller aux bureaux. Les cyclo-pousses et les tricycles à moteur, notamment, ont eu du mal à circuler sur cet axe avec les énormes trous en plein milieu de la chaussée, ainsi que les trous en « escalier», faisant parfois renverser des cyclo-pousses.Le ministère des Travaux publics a réhabilité 800 m de cette voie principale, longtemps en restée en mauvais état. « Les travaux de réhabilitation, partant du PK 925+000 jusqu’au PK 925+800, avancent à grands pas. La particularité de cette nouvelle chaussée est qu’elle est refaite en béton », note le ministère. La présence des dallots de déversement sur les côtés est également constatée. L’absence de ces ouvrages permettant l’écoulement de l’eau vers la mer a en effet longtemps fait défaut et contribué à accentuer les inondations dans cette partie de la ville.La réhabilitation est, jusqu’ici, réalisée à moitié. Toutefois, une voie, ayant rempli les conditions qu’il faut pour une chaussée en béton, est actuellement ouverte à la circulation. Elle avait été interdite au passage, même aux piétons, pendant un mois. Les travaux continuent avec le ferraillage, partant du rond-point jusqu’au bureau de la gendarmerie de Sanfily. Soit une partie de la plus belle avenue de Toliara, l’avenue « Monja Jaona ».Mirana Ihariliva

title: PVR Inox ordered to pay Rs 6,000 after movie show cancelled 10 minutes after start
content:
NEW DELHI: A Hyderabad district consumer commission has directed PVR Inox and an Inox theatre to pay Rs 6,000 to a customer after a movie show was cancelled about 10 minutes after it began. The commission found deficiency in service and unfair trade practice and awarded Rs 5,000 compensation and Rs 1,000 litigation costs. The order was passed on September 11, 2026.
Why did the customer approach the commission?According to the commission order, P Prashanth purchased a ticket for the Telugu film “Hongkong Warriors” for Rs 173 through BookMyShow on January 26, 2025. He reached the theatre on time and started watching the movie, but the show was cancelled about 10 minutes into the screening.
Prashanth alleged that the theatre initially said the show was cancelled because of low occupancy. He said the management later changed its explanation and said there was a technical issue. He claimed the sudden cancellation caused mental distress and inconvenience and that his complaints to BookMyShow and the theatre did not receive a satisfactory response.
He sought Rs 50,000 as compensation for deficiency in service, mental agony and harassment, besides Rs 25,000 towards litigation costs.
The theatre disputed the allegations. It said the show was cancelled because of a technical error caused by storage limitations in the screen's Audi 06. It said its engineering team tried to resolve the issue but could not do so. The theatre also said a 100 percent refund was offered along with an alternative movie experience. It said the refund was later processed and argued that no further compensation was payable.
What did the commission find?The bench of President
Vakkanti Narasimha Rao and member
Suma Vala noted that the theatre had not produced a technical report or other documentary evidence to support its claim that the show was cancelled because of a technical problem.
“The complainant is not in dispute that he arrived at the theatre on time and began watching the movie, however, about 10 minutes into the Screening, the theatre management abruptly cancelled the show on the initial ground due to low occupancy that was not believable,” the bench said.
The commission also noted that the theatre later gave a different reason for the cancellation. It said the theatre had relied on its written version and evidence affidavit but had not produced substantial documentary proof of the alleged technical problem.
“It is also not in dispute that, later the theatre management changed their version stating that ‘the cancellation was due to Technical issue’ that was under suspicious of the truthfulness and Bonafide’s of the Opposite Parties. Neither any technical report nor any technical error cropped-up caused by storage limitation in the Screen AUDI 06 was filed in support of the Contentions of Opposite Party,” it added.
The commission further noted that the ticket amount had been refunded after the show was cancelled. However, it said the refund did not remove the deficiency in service arising from the cancellation.
“It is also an admitted fact that the ticket cost was alleged to be refunded to the original payment mode on 27th January, 2025 under Ex. A-1 as the theatre management abruptly cancelled the show wherein it was mentioned that ‘Still haven’t received the refund’,” the commission further added.
The commission held that the cancellation amounted to deficiency in service and unfair trade practice. It partly allowed the complaint and awarded compensation and litigation costs.
What did the commission order?The Hyderabad district consumer commission directed PVR Inox and the theatre to:
- Pay Rs 5,000 as compensation for deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.
- Pay Rs 1,000 towards litigation costs.
- Pay the total Rs 6,000 jointly and severally.
- Make the payment within 45 days from receiving the order.
- The customer's remaining claims were disallowed.

title: Perceived faith-oriented public-space environments, activity participation, and social connectedness among older adults in Quanzhou Ancient City
content: Older adults’ perceptions of urban public spaces are associated with their outdoor activities and social interactions, whereas locally embedded folk culture is associated with distinctive patterns of spatial engagement. In the context of historic city renewal, understanding how culturally embedded environments are associated with social connectedness among older adults is essential. This study examines how environmental perceptions of public spaces are associated with social connectedness among older adults and tests the indirect associations through activity participation. Using Licheng District of Quanzhou Ancient City as the study area, a structural equation model was developed to analyze the path relationships among five dimensions of environmental perception—activity-oriented, landscape-oriented, accessibility-oriented, communicative, and faith-oriented elements—activity participation, and social connectedness. Data were obtained from two repeated cross-sectional surveys conducted in October 2020 and January 2024 (n = 620) and analyzed using structural equation modeling. After adjustment for gender, age, educational attainment, household composition, and religious affiliation, all five dimensions of environmental perception were positively associated with stronger social connectedness: activity-oriented (β = 0.100, p = 0.017), landscape-oriented (β = 0.157, p < 0.001), accessibility-oriented (β = 0.169, p < 0.001), communicative (β = 0.125, p = 0.001), and faith-oriented perception (β = 0.091, p = 0.022). Faith-based folk activities (β = 0.169), non-faith folk activities (β = 0.145), and non-folk activities (β = 0.180) were also positively associated with social connectedness (all p < 0.001). Bootstrap analyses identified activity-specific indirect associations between environmental perception and social connectedness. Given the repeated cross-sectional design, the findings indicate statistical associations rather than causal effects.

title: La lucha de Paco por universalizar el lenguaje del suelo para las personas ciegas: "Ser ciego no implica no saber dónde estás"
content:
La lucha de Paco por universalizar el lenguaje del suelo para las personas ciegas: "Ser ciego no implica no saber dónde estás"
Basado en hechos observados y verificados directamente por nuestros periodistas o por fuentes informadas.
Elígenos como tu fuente preferida en Google.
Paco Tello explica cómo funcionan las referencias tactovisuales y por qué sin accesibilidad no autonomía
Caminar sin ver, sin pisar. Botones y franjas en el suelo. Colores. Quienes no los necesitamos casi ni los vemos, ni los notamos bajo nuestros pies. Un buen día reparas, ¿qué será esto?
"Las referencias tactovisuales (así se llaman los botones, franjas y colores) son elementos de accesibilidad. Son herramientas de vista o tacto: se perciben al tacto del pie o del bastón. Estas referencias hacen accesible el entorno porque no lo es para las personas ciegas", explica Paco Tello, responsable de la unidad de autonomía personal y bienestar social de la ONCE. En el departamento de Paco se encargan de dar estrategias a las personas ciegas para que adquieran autonomía. Les enseñan a usar el bastón, el teléfono móvil o los electrodomésticos, por ejemplo. Pero ¿de qué sirve saber usarlos y tener un bastón, si el entorno no es accesible?
Paco tiene discapacidad visual y auditiva debido al síndrome de Usher. Es usuario de un perro guía llamado Garbi. Dice que él forma un equipo con su perro, trabajan juntos. Cuando Paco conoce el recorrido, coge protagonismo en relación a Garbi. Él sabe por dónde tiene que ir y en este caso no solo le ayuda el apoyo de su perro, sino también las referencias tactovisuales que debería haber en el suelo. Cuando no conoce un camino, estas herramientas, que pasan desapercibidas para los demás, le ayudan mucho, y también a su perro, que toma una mayor responsabilidad.
Las señales son tactovisuales porque no todo es tocar, también es ver. Paco tiene resto visual y para las personas como él existen estas referencias que se colocan en el suelo buscando el contraste de colores. "Yo vivo en Madrid y en el metro el suelo es muy oscuro y la referencia visual que ponen es amarilla. Después, ya nos encontramos con un tacto con rugosidad. Es eso que hace que la maleta haga ruido cuando pasa por encima: 'ru ru ru ru'. Nosotros cuando vamos con el bastón percibimos esa rugosidad después de ver la referencia visual y sabemos que viene una escalera", explica Paco. "Luego en los escalones hay una banda rugosa que al común de los mortales os sirve también como antideslizante, por lo que son elementos que nos valen a todos".
Las referencias tactovisuales sirven para alertar de la presencia de algún riesgo y también para dirigir a la persona ciega. No se llaman oficialmente botones, pero de manera coloquial se conoce como botonera a estos puntitos que nos encontramos en el suelo. "Por ejemplo, al borde del andén del metro y del tren la botonera nos avisa de que después hay una caída. Sabemos que está la botonera, después las bandas antideslizantes y luego las vías", apunta Paco.
Estas señales ayudan a que los ciegos puedan hacerse sus mapas en la cabeza porque "ser ciego no implica no saber dónde estás", cuenta. Por ejemplo, si él usara con frecuencia la estación de Chamartín, ya tendría aprendido algo así como que al entrar se encuentra con una textura de cruce de encaminamiento, tiene que coger el camino de la izquierda, seguir recto y en la segunda textura de cruce que se encuentre, girar en el encaminamiento de la derecha para llegar a las escaleras de bajada para la línea 1.
Una textura de cruce de encaminamiento vuelve a ser una botonera, pero esta vez de forma cuadrada para señalar un cruce de caminos: la posibilidad que tiene la persona ciega de ir en distintas direcciones, como aparece en la imagen de la parte superior de la página. La diferencia es que de este cruce salen encaminamientos, que son "pequeños carriles de líneas continuas también en relieve, como los botones. Lo ideal es que haya seis líneas en paralelo porque así sabes lo que es. Hay en estaciones, centros comerciales, etc. Los encaminamientos nos marcan el camino que tenemos que seguir", cuenta Paco.
Las botoneras también avisan de posibles peligros en la calle o de que se acerca un paso de cebra. También sirven para enfrentarse a las plataformas únicas, que son calles donde la acera y la carretera están a la misma altura. Como no hay bordillo, el bastón no distingue si estás en la carretera o no. "Si pones una banda de botonera entre la acera y la carretera nos ayudas, porque así nos señalas el fin de la acera. Esto no quiere decir que es un paso de cebra (si está bien hecho, claro). Solo te avisa de que se acaba la acera y empieza la carretera. Para que esté bien hecha, la botonera tiene que ocupar todo el ancho de la calle y llegar hasta la pared".
Es importante que las señales tactovisuales existan siempre y que sean las homologadas. Pasa que algún espabilado hace su botonera o su encaminamiento como cree conveniente y, por ejemplo, si las líneas rectas del encaminamiento están más pegadas de lo que deben estar, pueden resultar invisibles al tacto del bastón. Otro tema importante es no poner nada sobre la botonera y el encaminamiento.
"Recuerdo que en el camino a mi anterior trabajo, la Policía dejaba el furgón encima del encaminamiento. Que yo lo entiendo, que era verano y así estaba a la sombra, pero fui a hablar con ellos y explicárselo: entiendo que no sois conscientes, pero si me tapas el encaminamiento yo ahora cómo sigo, no sé hacia dónde tengo que ir. Y así con todo: obras, cubos de basura, motos, furgonetas de reparto, etc.".
"Sin accesibilidad no hay autonomía, van de la mano. Si no hay encaminamiento de qué me sirve el bastón si voy a cruzar por donde no debo, por ejemplo. Y sin autonomía no hay libertad. Será suficiente accesibilidad el día que las personas ciegas (en general para cualquier persona con discapacidad) lleguen donde llegan todos. Entonces será suficiente", reivindica.

title: Niño despertó de un coma de 16 días y la reacción del encuentro con su madre conmovió en redes sociales
content:
Un video en el que se observa cómo una madre corre a reencontrarse con su hijo de 8 años de edad, quien aguarda en una camilla luego de permanecer 16 días en coma, despertó las reacciones de miles de personas en redes sociales.
En la escena se puede observar cómo ambos se emocionan al verse nuevamente. Entre lágrimas, se abrazan fuertemente y dejan en evidencia la felicidad de volver a estar juntos después de varios días de incertidumbre.
Al ver a su madre, el pequeño grita emocionado y conmovido: “Mamá”, mientras ella lo abraza y llora al tenerlo nuevamente entre sus brazos.
Su familia calificó aquel momento como un “milagro”, después de que el menor estuviera cerca de perder la vida debido a una complicación de salud.
Un símbolo de resiliencia
Guilherme Gandra Moura, conocido cariñosamente como Menino Gui, es un niño brasileño que actualmente tiene 12 años y padece epidermólisis ampollosa, una enfermedad genética que provoca una extrema fragilidad de la piel.
Las personas que viven con algunas formas de esta condición son conocidas popularmente como 'niños mariposa', debido a que su piel puede ser tan delicada como las alas de este insecto.
En el caso de Guilherme, los pequeños roces, golpes o fricciones pueden provocar ampollas y heridas, por lo que debe enfrentar constantes cuidados y procedimientos médicos.
En 2023, cuando tenía 8 años, su estado de salud se complicó debido a una neumonía. Ante la gravedad de su condición, los médicos tuvieron que inducirlo a un coma que se prolongó durante 16 días.
Su despertar y el posterior reencuentro con su madre quedaron registrados en video. Las imágenes rápidamente se difundieron en redes sociales y convirtieron al pequeño en una figura conocida en Brasil.
Su madre, Tayane Gandra, ha destacado en diferentes ocasiones la fortaleza de su hijo y la actitud positiva con la que enfrenta las dificultades derivadas de su enfermedad.
Su amor por el fútbol
La historia de Guilherme también está estrechamente relacionada con su pasión por el fútbol y, especialmente, con el club brasileño CR Vasco da Gama.
Después de salir del hospital, el pequeño comenzó a ganar un lugar especial entre los aficionados y jugadores del equipo. Su vínculo con el club se fortaleció con el tiempo y llegó a convertirse en una de las figuras más queridas por la hinchada.
Su historia incluso trascendió las fronteras de Brasil. En diciembre de 2024, Guilherme recibió el Premio a la Afición de la FIFA, conocido como FIFA Fan Award, durante la ceremonia de los premios The Best.
El reconocimiento destacó su manera de vivir el fútbol como una fuente de alegría y fortaleza mientras enfrenta las dificultades relacionadas con su salud.
"Siento un amor inmenso por el Vasco. El Vasco me ayuda a olvidar las cosas malas y no siento ningún dolor. Lo único que tengo que decir es que mientras haya un corazón infantil, el Vasco será inmortal”, expresó el pequeño al hablar de su relación con el club.
Actualmente, Guilherme continúa compartiendo parte de su vida en redes sociales. Entre publicaciones relacionadas con su familia, el fútbol y sus procesos médicos, 'Menino Gui' sigue mostrando cómo ha convertido su historia en un mensaje de esperanza y resiliencia.

title: ¿Cómo se asignan las ayudas para reparar apartamentos afectados por los terremotos en La Guaira?
content:
Las autoridades nacionales comenzaron la entrega de ayudas económicas a propietarios de apartamentos y juntas de condominio afectados por los terremotos del 24 de junio en La Guaira. El programa contempla entre 1.500 y 5.000 dólares para reparaciones independientes dentro de las viviendas y hasta 20.000 dólares para trabajos en áreas comunes gestionados por las juntas de condominio.
En la primera fase en La Guaira fueron incluidos 1.647 propietarios vinculados a 57 juntas de condominio y 70 edificaciones. Estos inmuebles fueron clasificados con etiqueta amarilla por la Comisión Presidencial para la Evaluación de Habitabilidad de Infraestructuras.
Pero recibir la ayuda no significa que todos los propietarios obtengan 5.000 dólares. De hecho, en la primera entrega reportada en La Guaira se transfirieron 2.821,30 dólares a cada una de las 1.647 familias beneficiadas, mientras que medios locales señalaron que en Residencias Parque Mar algunos propietarios recibieron cantidades de entre 1.500 y 3.000 dólares, de acuerdo con reportes de La Verdad de Vargas.
¿Quién puede recibir la ayuda para reparar su apartamento?
El primer paso es que la vivienda aparezca en los registros realizados después de los sismos y que haya sido incluida en las evaluaciones de habitabilidad.
En el caso de la primera fase de La Guaira, los beneficiarios pertenecen a edificaciones que fueron evaluadas y clasificadas con etiqueta amarilla, dentro del proceso de revisión realizado por la Comisión Presidencial para la Evaluación de Habitabilidad de Infraestructuras.
Esto permite distinguir la ayuda de un pago general para todas las personas afectadas por los terremotos. La inscripción en el censo y la evaluación del inmueble forman parte del proceso para determinar quiénes pueden acceder al programa.
La gobernación ha informado que las juntas de condominio son parte importante de este proceso porque reúnen la información de los propietarios y la remiten a las autoridades. Por ello, una persona que no haya sido incluida en el primer listado puede necesitar verificar con su junta si sus datos fueron registrados y cuál es el procedimiento para incorporar su caso.
¿En qué se diferencian las ayudas para los apartamentos y los condominios?
Los recursos individuales están destinados a reparaciones dentro de cada vivienda. Por separado, el programa contempla financiamientos de hasta 20 mil dólares para las juntas de condominio registradas, destinados a intervenir las áreas comunes de los edificios.
Esto quiere decir que una misma residencia puede acceder a dos vías distintas de financiamiento. Un propietario puede recibir un subsidio para reparar su apartamento, mientras la junta puede gestionar recursos para trabajos en espacios compartidos.
Las áreas comunes pueden requerir intervenciones diferentes a las de cada vivienda, por lo que el financiamiento de la junta no se reparte entre los propietarios como si fuera un segundo bono individual.
¿Qué deben hacer quienes todavía no aparecen entre los beneficiarios?
Los propietarios que no fueron incluidos en la primera fase deben verificar con su junta de condominio si fueron incorporados al censo y si el inmueble fue sometido a la evaluación correspondiente.
La información recopilada por las juntas sirve para elaborar los listados que posteriormente son enviados a las autoridades. Por ello, no aparecer en la primera entrega no necesariamente significa que el proceso terminó para ese propietario.
Las autoridades han informado que el programa continuará con nuevas intervenciones y entregas. En La Guaira, además de las reparaciones individuales, se anunció la atención de más edificaciones y familias afectadas por los terremotos del 24 de junio.

title: Ten female entrepreneurs graduate from the Standard Chartered Foundation Women in Tech Accelerator
content:
Audio By Carbonatix
Standard Chartered Bank Ghana PLC held the Pitch Day and Graduation ceremony for the sixth cohort of its Women in Tech programme, celebrating ten women entrepreneurs who completed the programme and pitched their businesses for a share of the grant funding.
The five top-performing businesses, Edu3Dcation, WADMET, Verte Tower, SisiMarie and Porducare, will each receive GH₵113,500 in grant funding to support the growth and scaling of their climate-smart, technology-enabled ventures, which address local and broader market needs.
The programme is implemented by the Ghana Climate Innovation Centre, a centre within Ashesi University, which supports entrepreneurs through business and skills development and connections to the wider innovation ecosystem. Over six months, the Standard Chartered Foundation Women in Tech (SCFWIT) Accelerator combined practical learning with dedicated portfolio management support, masterclasses, pitch preparation and networking opportunities, equipping women-led, technology-driven businesses with the tools and resources they need to grow.
Building on the achievements of its first five cohorts, the programme has provided USD 210,000 in grants and supported 83 women-led businesses. These businesses have created more than 166 jobs, reached over 31,231 customers and generated GH₵3.9 million in cumulative revenue, demonstrating the contribution of women entrepreneurs to Ghana’s technology and climate innovation ecosystem.
The Pitch Day and Graduation brought together investors, ecosystem leaders, alumni and partners to recognise the cohort’s progress and create opportunities for the entrepreneurs to build relationships that will support the growth of their businesses.
Pearl Esua-Mensah, Executive Director of the Ghana Climate Innovation Centre (GCIC), said: “Cohort Six reached further than any before it, into regions the accelerator had not yet touched, including women living with disabilities. Our mission at GCIC is to build the entrepreneurs, leaders and institutions Africa needs to scale climate solutions. That mission means nothing if it only reaches those already closest to opportunity. Every founder graduating today is a bet that talent is not concentrated in one region and that a woman with the right technology can compete with anyone, anywhere.”
The event featured pitches from all ten entrepreneurs, who demonstrated how they are applying technology and innovation to address challenges and opportunities in their respective sectors.
Xorse Godzi, Chief Executive of Standard Chartered Bank Ghana PLC, reiterated the bank's commitment to supporting women entrepreneurs, saying: “Our commitment to the Women in Tech accelerator aligns with our belief that empowering female-led businesses leveraging technology is critical to building more competitive and sustainable enterprises. By enabling women-led businesses to harness the full potential of technology, we are helping create more resilient enterprises, unlock new opportunities and drive sustainable economic development”.
Guest of Honour Theresa Ayoade, Chief Executive Officer of Charterhouse, reflected on her own entrepreneurial journey and the importance of perseverance and support, saying: “Vision is lonely at the beginning. It always is. Perseverance is not a strategy; it is survival. But you also need a platform that gives you the opportunity to grow. Whether it is a music awards stage or a business incubation programme, you cannot grow alone. What matters is having the courage to pursue your vision and the right people and platforms to help you take it further.”

title: Håkon (17) var sikker på at han hadde ADHD. Hjelpen forandret alt.
content:
Håkon (18) var sikker på at han hadde ADHD.
Men hjelpen han fikk, forandret alt.
Slik hjelp får ikke alle barn.
ADHD-lotteriet
ADHD-lotteriet
NRK har kartlagt bruken av ADHD-medisin blant barn i Norge.
Vi oppdaget at den varierer kraftig, etter hvor barna bor.
I noen kommuner bruker nesten ti ganger så mange barn ADHD-medisin som i andre.
Andelen barn som bruker ADHD-medisin etter kommune.
Forskjellene er enorme fra kommune til kommune.
I kommunen med høyest bruk får hvert tiende barn ADHD-medisin.
I kommunen med lavest bruk får hvert hundrede barn ADHD-medisin.
Kommuner med færre enn ti barn på ADHD-medisin er utelatt av hensyn til personvernet. Kilde: FHI
Nederst i saken kan du se tallene for flere kommuner.
Hvorfor er forskjellene så store?
Vi dro til kommunen med lavest medisinbruk.
Gutten som trodde han hadde ADHD
I Lørenskog møter vi Håkon.
Her bruker bare rundt én prosent av barna ADHD-medisin.
Håkon er 18 år og jobber som tømrerlærling på en byggeplass.
– Jeg synes det er veldig gøy. Det er mye bedre enn motparten, altså skole og sånt, sier han.
For noen år siden slet han med uro og konsentrasjonsvansker. Han følte seg annerledes enn de andre og slet med å passe inn.
– På skolen var jeg ofte ukonsentrert. Jeg var urolig. Klarte ikke følge med på det læreren sa, forteller Håkon.
Etter hvert ble han sikker i sin sak.
– Jeg var overbevist om at jeg hadde ADHD, forteller han.
Også moren hans tenkte det samme.
– Vi ønsket et svar på hvorfor hverdagen var så vanskelig, sier mamma Nancy Gogstad.
Men hun ringte ikke først til BUP, barne- og ungdomspsykiatrien, som utreder ADHD.
Hun ringte til kommunen.
Der fikk hun tak i Renate Horgheim Bjercke.
Vendepunktet
Bjercke er psykologspesialist i Lørenskog kommune og jobber i et lavterskel tilbud for psykisk helse for barn.
Her kan familier ta kontakt, uten å gå via fastlegen.
Hjelpen er gratis.
Bjercke hadde samtaler med Håkon. Hun veiledet foreldrene og ga råd til lærerne hans på skolen.
– Det at vi kunne ringe direkte til en psykolog og få hjelp med en gang, det var kjempeviktig, sier mamma Nancy Gogstad.
Hun mener lavterskeltilbudet ble avgjørende for sønnen.
Han kom seg over kneika. Han hadde ingen ADHD-diagnose. Han trengte ikke medisiner.
– Renate hjalp meg utrolig mye. Jeg fikk et sted å tømme meg for vonde tanker. Jeg slapp å gå bære på det, sier Håkon.
I Lørenskog sier fagfolk at tidlig hjelp kan bidra til at færre barn henvises til ADHD-utredning.
– Barn kan streve med uro av andre grunner enn ADHD. Det kan vi nøste i tidlig, så barnet får riktig hjelp, sier Renate Horgheim Bjercke.
Men slik hjelp finnes ikke overalt.
Mer medisin i distriktene
Når vi ser nærmere på tallene, oppdager vi et geografisk mønster:
Jo mindre sentral kommunen er, jo flere barn får ADHD-medisin.
I mindre sentrale kommuner er andelen dobbelt så høy som i sentrale kommuner.
Hvert tolvte barn på medisin
400 kilometer unna Lørenskog ligger Røros, en landlig kommune sør i Trøndelag.
Den ligger høyt på NRKs liste over medisinbruk.
Her går rundt 8 prosent av barna på ADHD-medisin, altså hvert tolvte barn.
Det er nesten tre ganger høyere enn landsgjennomsnittet.
– Lite hjelp
– 8 prosent! Det er sjokkerende! utbryter Linda Cathrine Herud.
Tre foreldre sitter samlet i en sofa i velhuset på Røros.
Alle har barn som har fått ADHD-diagnose.
De er ikke mot medisiner, men mener barna deres har fått for lite annen hjelp.
– Jeg følte at vi fikk veldig lite hjelp på skolen. Og da mener jeg veldig lite hjelp, sier Kjell Morten Hansen.
– Jeg føler det eneste vi har fått hjelp til, er rett og slett medisineringen. Alle andre tiltak har vi måtte finne ut av selv, sier Monika Goodwine.
Linda Cathrine Herud er enig.
– Det finnes ikke god nok tilrettelegging for alle som sliter på skolen, sier hun.
Hun understreker at noen barn helt klart trenger medisiner.
– Men jeg tror også at det noen ganger er enkleste veien ut, sier Linda Cathrine Herud.
Kortere vei til tablett?
– Nei, det var overraskende tall, sier Vegar Dahl om NRKs kartlegging.
Han er leder av barne- og ungdomspsykiatrisk poliklinikk, BUP, på Røros.
Det er hit barn kommer for utredning, diagnose og behandling.
De siste årene har antall henvisninger for ADHD eksplodert her, forteller Dahl.
– Vi vet at 50 prosent av barna i BUP har en ADHD-diagnose, sier han.
Den høye medisinbruken bekymrer.
Han har en forklaring.
– I flere år har det vært et mangelfullt lavterskeltilbud for barn og unges psykiske helse i Røros, sier han.
Røros er en fattig kommune, og det er få ressurser til ekstra tiltak for barn som sliter, ifølge Dahl.
– Da øker presset på å medisinere, både fra foreldre og skole som ønsker at barnet skal få hjelp, forklarer han.
– Betyr det at det er lettere å gi tablett enn tiltak?
– Terskelen for å gi medisin vil være lavere, hvis man ikke har andre tiltak, svarer Dahl.
– Er det tilfelle her?
– Det kan se sånn ut, sier han.
Dahl understreker at medisiner kan ha god effekt for mange.
Men fagmiljøet er bekymret for den høye bruken.
– Jeg tror at hvis vi hadde hatt bedre tiltak i førstelinjetjenesten, så hadde vi medisinert mindre, sier Dahl.
Han mener hjelpen barna får, henger sammen med hvor de bor.
– Det er store ressursforskjeller mellom kommuner i Norge. Det fører til at barn får ulikt tilbud og ulik oppfølging.
Tidlig hjelp – færre diagnoser
En fersk rapport utarbeidet på oppdrag fra Helsedirektoratet peker i samme retning.
Den har sett på hjelpen barn får i kommunene, og hvor mange som får ADHD.
Mønsteret er tydelig: Kommuner som bruker mer på veiledning og forebygging, har færre barn med ADHD.
Folkehelseinstituttet (FHI) ser det samme.
– Små kommuner med få ressurser til forebygging har ofte flere diagnoser og mer bruk av medisiner, sier Heidi Aase. Hun er avdelingsdirektør i FHI.
Hun påpeker at andre trekk, som befolkningssammensetning, også kan bidra til forskjellene.
– Unger burde ha like muligheter
I sofaen på velhuset blir foreldrene opprørte over forskjellene.
To av dem har barn som har blitt ung ufør.
De mener tidligere hjelp kunne gjort en forskjell for barna.
– Jeg tror det hadde vært som dag og natt, sier Linda Cathrine Herud
– Det burde jo ikke være sånn. Ungene våre burde ha like muligheter som alle andre, sier hun.
– Ikke alltid vi lykkes
Ingvild Prøsch-Moen er kommunalsjef for oppvekst i Røros. Hun sier det er trist å høre at foreldre mener de ikke får hjelpen de trenger.
– Det er ikke bestandig vi lykkes. Det erkjenner vi, sier Prøsch-Moen.
Hun avviser samtidig at det ikke har vært tiltak rundt barn som strever.
Men Røros har hittil ikke hatt et lavterskeltilbud for barn og unge, som det de har i Lørenskog.
– Men det er i oppstartsfasen nå. Der kan barn og foreldre selv ta kontakt, forteller Prøsch-Moen.
– Takknemlig
Tilbake i Lørenskog borer Håkon hull til viftekanal i et nybygg.
18-åringen fra Lørenskog vil fortelle historien sin fordi han vet at det kan gå bra. Han ønsker at andre barn skal få samme mulighet.
– Hvis jeg ikke hadde fått den hjelpa, hadde jeg mest sannsynlig ikke vært i det yrket jeg var i nå. Så jeg er utrolig glad for at jeg er det og fikk den hjelpa, sier Håkon.
Her kan du sjekke din kommune
Hold over kartet for å se hvor mange barn som bruker ADHD-medisin.
Kommuner der færre enn ti jenter eller gutter bruker medisin, er anonymisert.
Landsgjennomsnittet er på 2,68 prosent.
Forskjellene er store
Se hvem som er på topp og bunn.
